zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0. Supplied index: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription and explanatory notes are this reviewer's scan-based work; the index is an identification aid, not diplomatic authority.

runs.text: mãos poſto que cada hum enteado em reſpeito

lines.note: Mãos completes ir-/mãos from the preceding page in the definition of step-siblings. Each child is a stepchild in relation to one member of the newly married couple; the sentence continues below.
Completes the reference to the wife and husband. This closes the Iqiai qiodai entry begun on f0268, not a new headword on this page.
Ikikaeru is to return to life or revive, intransitively. The upright initial I and the c in Reſuſcitar replace damaged OCR; the following entry provides the corresponding transitive verb.
Ikikaesu means to restore someone to life. The extra initial A in the OCR is not printed; a alguem distinguishes the transitive meaning from the preceding entry.
The two forms describe labored breathing. Tra- begins trabalho, and the examples below explain the kind of breathlessness intended rather than supplying another sense.

runs.text: balho como o que tem aſma, ou ſobe algũa la-

lines.note: Completes trabalho and compares the breathing to that of someone with asthma or someone climbing a slope. The historical spelling aſma is retained.
Completes ladeira grande, a large or steep slope. This closes the second illustration of labored breathing.
Ikidowori denotes resentment or indignation with fury and anger. The printed internal ouo sequence is preserved, rather than replaced by a modern romanization.
Ikidowori wo sanzuru, dispelling or venting one's resentment, is glossed as taking revenge. The s in ſanzuru is the Japanese long-s type, not f.
The related verb means to harbor hatred with anger and fury. Furor corrects the OCR fucor, and the initial is an upright capital I.

This redirects the shorter adjective to the preferred Iqidauaxij above. Meliùs is one italic editorial word, not the draft's fragmented mixture of fonts; the headword begins with I, not a stray long s.
Ikihiki is asthma, with iki wo hiku as the associated expression. The f in fiqu is a Japanese h-row spelling, not long s; doẽ- begins the word for being ill.
Completes doẽte de aſma: suffering from asthma. The abbreviated nasal marking in the preceding fragment is retained rather than expanded.

Ikigai mo nai is illustrated with a person, and the Portuguese begins Homem across the row boundary. The explanation below concerns the supposed usefulness of the person's living; it is the historical dictionary's gloss, not an added evaluation.

runs.text: mem que não aproueita nada viuendo.

lines.note: Completes the gloss as a person whose being alive is of no benefit. No hyphen is supplied between Ho and mem because the preceding row has none securely printed.
Ikigawa is the skin of a living creature. Repetition of the noun begins the example continued below; the headword's capital I replaces the draft's lowercase recognition.
Completes ikigawa wo hagu, removing skin from a living creature. Esfolar has the meaningful f of the Portuguese verb; the Japanese f likewise belongs to the printed h-row spelling.
Ikigao is the face of a person while alive. The example begins with Voya, parent, wholly in roman type; the final a is printed and there is no line-end hyphen, unlike the garbled draft Voy-.

runs.text: Ver o roſto do pay an

lines.note: Completes the example about seeing one's parent's living face; the Portuguese specifies the father. Ver and the article o are separated by a visible narrow gap. An continues into antes below without an added hyphen.
Completes antes de morrer, seeing the father before he dies. This is the end of the example, not part of the following verb for emerging alive.
Iki ide/izuru means to come out alive. Fu- begins futa toqi, the time expression in the cited example, and is kept as a physical word fragment.

runs.text: ta toqi bacari atte mina iqi ide tamayeri.

lines.note: Completes the Japanese example: after about two time units, all emerged alive. The honorific tamayeri remains as printed; the historical Portuguese rendering of the time interval is on the next two rows.

The roman citation label Taif. is followed by book 26 and a translation beginning after about two hours. The source's horas rendering is recorded without converting historical toqi into a modern clock duration; Paßadas retains the double-s ligature.
Completes horas and states that all came out alive. The tilded ſairão is retained as the source's spelling in this past-event translation.

runs.text: Modo de eſtar algũa couſa viua, eſ-

lines.note: Ikiiki to describes being lively or fresh. The scan shows two consecutive i types after the first q, consistent with the subsequently consulted NINJAL entry 133a12; neither is dropped. Eſ- begins eſperta below.
Completes eſperta and compares the condition with fresh grass or flowers. The dictionary applies the same vividness to a person in the following example.

Ikiiki to shita hito is an alert or lively person. The example repeats Iqiiqito with two narrow consecutive i types after the first q; this replaces the draft Iquqito and agrees with the independently reinspected headword.
Ikimi denotes a living person. The capital I and the Portuguese double-s ligature are retained, keeping this short entry distinct from the following feast.

runs.text: Cõuite q̃ fazem os parentes, ou os

lines.note: Ikimitama names a feast or offering for living people. The Portuguese begins with relatives and continues with the recipients and occasion below; the headword starts with I, not OCR A.

runs.text: filhos a ſeus pais, ou criados aos ſenhores no

lines.note: Identifies children honoring parents and servants honoring their masters. The clause continues into the season of the commemoration of the dead, rather than describing an ordinary meal.

runs.text: tempo da commemoração dos defuntos em

lines.note: Places the observance during the commemoration of the dead. The following phrase explains that the feast nevertheless congratulates people who are still alive.
Completes the explanation as a celebration of their continued life. The printed wording is retained without adding a modern festival name or calendar date.
Ikimono is a living thing. The second sense is introduced as an occasional metaphorical use, with per continuing into met on the next physical row.
Completes the metaphorical-use label and applies the word to a lively or alert person. Peßoa retains the printed double-s ligature.
Ikinagarae means continuing to live or surviving, though the Portuguese gloss is simply to live. The printed principal forms and internal garaye sequence are preserved.
This headword denotes a pleasant fragrance, with an example about a scent spreading. The initial is capital I, and Re starts recender across the physical line boundary without a supplied hyphen.
Completes the fragrance-spreading gloss and introduces an example in which the scent remains in the room or seat. The cited translation follows on the next row.

The citation points to book 10 and explains that the zashiki remains fragrant. Zaxiqui is a Japanese room term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is retained in its locally printed italic setting; recenden continues below.
Completes recendendo and closes the example. The final upright S is the written-usage label and is not part of the italic Portuguese word.

runs.text: Demonio que entra no corpo dalguem

lines.note: Ikiryo is described in the dictionary's religious vocabulary as a demon entering someone's body. The following row identifies it with a living person; the printed reǒ is not modernized to a different romanization.

runs.text: nomeandoſe por algũa peßoa que eſtà viua.

lines.note: Completes the account of the possessing spirit as identifying itself with a person who is still alive. Nomeandoſe corrects OCR nomcandoſe; the Portuguese presents a reported supernatural explanation rather than ordinary bodily life.

This verb is illustrated by mi ga ikiru, the body becoming heated. The Portuguese starts a description of having fever, completed on the next row; it is a distinct sense from the earlier verb meaning to live.
Completes the gloss as being feverish or heated. The historical eſquentado spelling and the f in febre are preserved.
Ikisugi here means to live a long time. The printed principal-form suffix is ru, distinguishing this entry from the following homonymous motion expression.
The next verb means to go on or pass ahead, and the dictionary recommends the yuki- form. Two long-s types are visible in Paſſar, correcting the single-s OCR; the Japanese Yu- continues below.
Completes yukisuguru, the preferred alternative to the preceding motion verb. This Japanese continuation is roman, not an isolated Portuguese gloss.
Ikita mono is a living thing. The space between the two Japanese words is retained, keeping this phrased expression distinct from the earlier single headword Iqimono.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: The final Q is printed upside down, with its tail above the bowl. It is represented as Q; the format does not encode type rotation.

lines.note: Ikitsugu here denotes labored breathing. Resfolegar requires the visible f, not the OCR long s; the comparison continues through the next two rows.

runs.text: quem eſtà muito canſado, ou como peixe que eſ

lines.note: Compares this breathing to extreme exhaustion or to a fish out of water. Eſ continues into eſtà below with no added line-end hyphen.

Completes the fish-out-of-water comparison. The upright S marks written usage, then the Portuguese explicitly supplies a spoken expression beginning Iqiuo. This row is indented with the surrounding continuation, rather than flush as in the provisional layout.
Completes the spoken expression iki wo tsugu mentioned within the preceding Portuguese explanation. The row remains an indented continuation and is not a new headword.

Ikitoworu means passing through some place. The printed form Iqitouori starts with capital I, not t; Meli- introduces a preferred alternative on the next row. Paßar uses a double-s ligature here, unlike the separate long-s pair in c1-l045.
Completes Meliùs and gives yukitoworu as the preferred form. The Latin editorial fragment is italic while the Japanese alternative remains roman.

The phrase refers collectively to all living sentient beings. Printed Iqitoxe corresponds to ikitose and is retained rather than replaced by the modern expression ikitoshi; the Portuguese qualification ſen- continues into ſenſitiuos below.
Completes the word for sentient beings. It closes the collective living-creatures expression before the following adverbial entry.

The entry is an adverb equated with Cuuaxǔ and glossed as finely or handsomely. Adu. is italic grammatical apparatus; the upright final S marks written usage. The Japanese synonym is not an embedded Portuguese term.

Ikioi is vigor or impetus. The example begins tsuwamono, soldiers, divided after mo-; the provisional narrow separation after the initial T is retained as spacing, not interpreted as a separate abbreviation.
Completes tsuwamono no ikioi ga tsukita: the soldiers' vigor ran out. Im- begins the Portuguese impeto repeated in the translation.
Completes the translation as the ending of the soldiers' impetus and vigor. This is a single Japanese example continued across three physical rows.

runs.text: Retrato viuo, ou pintura bem ti-

lines.note: Ikiutsushi is a lifelike portrait or picture drawn faithfully from life. The final ti- begins tirada, describing how the likeness was taken.
Completes the likeness-from-life definition and gives ikiutsushi ni kaku, drawing lifelike. Pin starts pintar below, without a securely printed hyphen.

runs.text: tar ao viuo, ou pello natural.

lines.note: Completes pintar and explains drawing from life or from nature. The historical doubled l in pello is retained.
Ikiyakana describes something very lively or fresh. The following row supplies grass and flowers as comparisons before extending the meaning to a person.
Completes the comparisons with plants and flowers, then explicitly marks a metaphorical application to a person. Peſ- begins peſſoa with its two long-s types divided between rows.
Completes peſſoa and gives a lively, alert person as the metaphorical sense. The initial long s belongs to the split Portuguese word, not to a Japanese headword.
Ikiyakani is identified only as the adverb corresponding to the preceding adjective. Adu. is italic grammatical information; no unattested separate gloss is added.
Ikizashi is the manner of breathing. The Portuguese resfolegar is visibly continuous here, unlike the OCR's inserted internal space; the Japanese example continues after the line-final hyphen.

runs.text: O modo de deitar o folego, ou reſ

lines.note: Completes ikizashi ga warui, describing poor or abnormal breathing. Reſ begins respirar across the next row; the printed line ends without a hyphen.
Completes respirar and states that the breathing is bad. Ruim, clearly visible, corrects OCR raim.
Ikizzumu describes straining or bearing down. The examples below concern bowel straining and difficult childbirth, not merely ordinary breathing.

runs.text: tem camaras de puxos, ou como molher que tẽ

lines.note: Gives bowel straining and a woman in labor as comparisons. Molher restores the clearly printed h missing from OCR moler, and the tilded tẽ remains unexpanded.
Completes the difficult-childbirth comparison, explaining the forceful straining meant by the preceding verb. This is the dictionary's description, not a medical instruction.
Ikizzuku means to gasp or breathe. Va- begins the named subject of a literary example, continued on the next row rather than forming another headword.

runs.text: dacuſuno qi qiuo vxinaite, vuono doro

lines.note: The passage describes losing spirit and begins a comparison with a fish in mud. The Portuguese below treats the preceding Va-/dacuſuno qi sequence as a man's name; its unusual printed spacing is retained without imposing a modern personal-name identification.
Completes the simile as gasping like a fish in mud, then cites Taif., book 34. The label and its period are roman; Lib. and the number are italic apparatus, with the final printed period restored.

runs.text: Este homem aßi chamado perdendo o animo

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the named subject as this man so called and says that he lost heart. This supports treating the preceding Japanese sequence as a name, while aßi retains the printed double-s ligature.

runs.text: eſtaua como peixe na lama esbofando.

lines.note: Completes the simile as a fish gasping in mud. The word is esbofando with f, not OCR esboſando; the visible cross-stroke and the breathing sense support the correction.

Ira and iragusa are names for nettles, with Voira qualified as local usage. The enlarged initial I belongs to IRa and spans two rows; the draft omitted it and inserted an extra i in iraguſa. Alicubi is italic editorial Latin, not Japanese text.
Completes ortigas and gives equivalent expressions for nettles stinging. The lower part of the enlarged I at the left belongs to the preceding row; this continuation starts with italic gas.
Completes the Portuguese subject: the nettles sting. It closes the example from the preceding two rows.
Irabakasu means to mock or ridicule. The printed rn in Eſcarnecer was collapsed by OCR into m; zom- begins the synonymous Portuguese verb zombar below.

Completes zombar, with upright B marking a low or vulgar expression. The Portuguese then mentions the Cami region and its equivalent Xebiracaſu; both Japanese mentions occur within that explanatory sentence, not in a standalone example.
Iraka is explained through iye no tsuma and glossed as a roof ridge or roof. The following row qualifies it as the roof of a tile-covered house.
Completes the tiled-roof definition and begins iraka wo naraburu, setting roofs alongside one another. The Japanese nara- continues into buru below.

runs.text: Igualar os tectos das caſas, fazendo

lines.note: Completes naraburu and explains aligning the roofs of houses. The phrase continues with the resulting display or mass of houses, rather than prescribing a building method.
Completes the image of many houses forming an array. This closes the roof-alignment example.

Irafidoi describes a frantic, petty or fussy person in the Portuguese explanation. The final co- begins the further characterizing adjective on the next row; no modernized Japanese spelling is imposed.
Completes comechoſo, the final adjective in the description of an irritable or restless person. The source spelling is retained rather than replaced by a modern Portuguese synonym.
Iragusa is nettles, repeated as its own headword after the earlier alternatives under IRa. Its capital I and long s are visible in the scan.
Irai can mean from this point onward, and the entry also gives a sense extending up to the present. The historical contracted Tègora is retained with its grave accent.
Completes the until-now sense and gives yosho yori irai, since childhood. Both o vowels in Yôxô carry circumflexes; Deſ- begins the Portuguese desde below.

Completes the translation as from childhood until now. Menino and atègora replace OCR mexino and atigora. The first n of menino is clogged and partly damaged, but its surviving shoulder and the nearby n type support this adopted reading; the uncertainty is retained. Atègora has a visible grave-marked e, comparable to Tègora above.
